questions.question_text: A patient with epilepsy is concerned about medication related weight gain. Which of the following epilepsy medications is associated with weight loss?
questions.explanation:
The generally accepted figure for the prevalence of schizophrenia in adults with a learning disability is 3%. Remember that this 
is three times that found in the general population (this fact appears in other questions!). 
Learning disability (co-morbidity) 
The point prevalence of mental health problems (including problem behaviour) in adults with learning disability lies between 30 
and 50%. 
 
The estimated prevalence rates in adults with learning disabilities for specific mental health problems taken from a population-
based study by Cooper (2007), are illustrated in the table below. 
 
Associated disorder Prevalence 
Psychotic disorder 4% 
Affective disorder 6% 
ADHD 1.5% 
Personality disorder 1% 
Anxiety disorder 4% 
Obsessive-compulsive disorder 0.7% 
Autism 7.5% 
Problem behaviour 22.5% 
 
The following key points are worth noting regarding psychiatric illness in people with learning disability. 
 Major depressive disorder occurs and can be diagnosed at all IQ levels though the diagnosis is easily missed or simply 
seen as challenging behaviour. 
 People with learning disabilities are more vulnerable to the adverse effects of loss life events, and so more likely to 
develop adjustment disorder. 
 PTSD is at least as common in people with learning difficulties. 
 Stimulant drugs are thought to be less effective in children with learning disability. They are relatively contraindicated in 
Tourette's and autism where they may precipitate tics. 
 
A patient with epilepsy is concerned about medication related weight gain. Which of the following epilepsy 
medications is associated with weight loss? 
 Valproate 
 Carbamazepine 
 Phenytoin 
 Lamotrigine 
 Topiramate 
 Correct answer :  Topiramate 
Topiramate 
Topiramate is used in epilepsy and in bipolar affective disorder as a mood stabiliser. It inhibits voltage gated sodium channels, therefore 
suppresses action potentials. In addition it increases GABA levels. 
 
Topiramate is unusual in that its use is associated with weight loss (most psychotropic drugs are associated with weight gain).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a tool used to assist in the diagnosis of autism that uses information gathered directly from the assessment of the individual suspected of having the condition?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Sep 2011 
 
The CSBQ (Children's Social Behaviour Questionnaire) is a caregiver based questionnaire used to establish the presence of 
pervasive developmental disorder symptoms. 
 
The PDDBI (Pervasive Developmental Disorder Behaviour Inventory) is a parent or caregiver completed rating scale. 
 
Autism (adult assessment) 
NICE Guidelines 
 
The following table gives details of the assessment tools recommended by NICE to aid more complex diagnosis and 
assessment for adults with suspected autistic spectrum disorder. 
 
Tool Description 
ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) Semi-structured interview of caregivers of individuals with autism 
Administration time is 1.5-2.5 hours. Recommended by NICE for those with a learning 
disability 
ADOS-G (Autism Diagnostic Observation 
Schedule-Generic) 
Semistructured assessment. Involves the use of observational schedules. Patients are 
engaged in specific activities and their behaviour observed. Recommended by NICE 
Tool Description 
for those with a learning disability 
AAA (Adult Asperger Assessment) A three part diagnostic instrument consisting of two screening instruments, the 
Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) and the Empathy Quotient (EQ), and a clinician-
conducted diagnostic questionnaire, the Adult Asperger Assessment (AAA) 
ASDI (Asperger Syndrome (and high-functioning 
autism) Diagnostic Interview 
An investigator-based interview diagnostic developed specifically for the assessment 
of Asperger syndrome (AS) in children and adults. This brief structured interview 
consists of 20 items divided into six broader areas of behavior that may be indicative 
of AS 
(RAADS-R) Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic 
Scale Revised 
An 80-item self-rating diagnostic scale for adults with average or above average 
intelligence 
 
To organise and structure the process of a more complex assessment, consider using a formal assessment tool, such as the 
Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders (DISCO), the ADOS-G or the ADI-R.

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of Prader-Willi syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome 
Prader-Willi syndrome results from deletion of genetic material from the chromosome 15 inherited of paternal origin, and is a classic example 
of imprinting. 
 
Typical features include:- 
 Hyperphagia (excessive eating) and obesity 
 Short stature 
 Delayed puberty, hypogonadism, infertility 
 Learning difficulties 
 Compulsive behaviour (e.g. skin picking)

questions.question_text: What is the average full scale IQ in Turner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Turner syndrome 
Turner syndrome occurs when one of the two X chromosomes that are found in females is completely or partially missing. It therefore only 
occurs in females. The process tends to occur randomly (can be either from the father or the mother) and does not predict additional risk in 
future siblings.  
 
This may seem odd as you will be aware of the process of X-inactivation (Lyonization) whereby one X chromosome is inactivated in each cell. 
This might lead you to suspect that having only one X chromosome is okay. The reason having just one X chromosome is an issue is that in 
X-inactivation not all genes are inactivated in the inactivated X chromosome. 
 
Features include:- 
 Short stature 
 Webbed neck 
 Broad chest (widely spaced nipples) 
 Gonadal dysfunction (amenorrhoea and infertility) 
 Congenital heart disease (cardiac malformation in approx 1/3 of cases) 
 Hypothyroidism 
 
Girls with Turner syndrome typically have a reasonably normal intelligence (mean full scale IQ of 90), however, they may have 
difficulty with nonverbal, social, and psychomotor skills.

questions.question_text: Regarding Prader-Willi syndrome, which of the following is true?

options.text: It is also known as happy puppet syndrome
Affected individuals typically have small gonads
It results from unexpressed genes on the chromosome of maternal origin
Affected females tend to retain fertility

correct_answer.text: Affected individuals typically have small gonads

questions.explanation:
Genomic imprinting 
Genomic imprinting refers to a situation where a piece of DNA can behave differently depending on whether it is inherited from 
the mother or the father. DNA sequences are marked (imprinted) in the ovaries and testes almost like a stamp which says 
where the sequence has come from, this stamp affects the expression of the sequence. The two classic examples in psychiatry 
include Prader-Willi and Angelman syndrome. 
 
Prader-Willi is due to a deletion of chromosome 15q when inherited from the father. It is characterised by hypotonia, short 
stature, polyphagia, obesity, small gonads, and mild mental retardation. 
 
Angelman's syndrome (Happy puppet syndrome) is due to a deletion of 15q when inherited from the mother. It is 
characterised by an unusually happy demeanour, developmental delay, seizures, sleep disturbance, and jerky hand 
movements.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with paradoxical reactions in people with learning difficulties?
questions.explanation:
Benzodiazepines (paradoxical reactions) 
Benzodiazepines are associated with paradoxical reactions (aka disinhibitory reactions) which are unexpected increases in aggressive 
behaviour, sexual disinhibition, hyperactivity, vivid dreams, and hostility. 
 
Its difficult to be sure how common they are as study findings vary widely (1%-58%). 
 
The following factors increase the risk of such reactions:- 
 Learning disability 
 Extremes of age (elderly or young) 
 History of aggression or poor impulse control 
 Benzodiazepine with short half life 
 High dose benzodiazepine 
 Intravenous administration of benzodiazepine 
 
Paradoxical reactions must be recorded. If they are severe it is advisable to avoid future use of benzodiazepines.

questions.question_text: Regarding learning disability, select the correct definition of the term impairment. A person of low general intelligence who possesses an unusually high skill in some special tasks

options.text: Loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function.
Lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human
Disadvantage for an individual that limits or prevents the fulfilment of a role that is normal for them
The failure of an individual to recognise their true potential

correct_answer.text: Loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function.

questions.explanation:
Learning disability (terms) 
The terms impairment, disability and handicap are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. In the WHO schedule they 
are not interchangeable. 
 
Impairment is any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function.  
 
Disability is any restriction or lack (resulting from impairment) of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range 
considered normal for a human being.  
 
Handicap is a disadvantage for an individual, resulting from an impairment or a disability, that limits or prevents the fulfilment of 
a role that is normal according to age, sex and social and cultural factors for that individual.

questions.question_text: Excessive appetite and obesity are characteristic of which of the following?
What is the most common cause of PTSD in people with learning difficulties?

options.text: Being a victim of violent crime

questions.explanation:
The more deliberate a trauma is perceived to be, the more likely it is to result in PTSD. This is true for both people with and 
without learning difficulties. 
Post traumatic stress disorder (learning difficulties) 
Presentation 
 
The presentation of PTSD in people with learning difficulties varies depending on their ability to think and communicate. 
 
In the able population the most common presenting features are nightmares, jumpiness, and sleep disturbance. In the learning disability 
population, the most common presenting feature is aggression and behavioral disturbance.  
 
Additional features include:- 
 Disruptive/defiant behavior 
 Self-harm 
 Agitation/jumpiness 
 Distractibility 
 Sleep problems 
 Depressed mood 
 
Nature of traumatic event 
 
Abuse is the commonest aetiological factor in the onset of PTSD disorder in people with learning difficulties. 
 
Management 
 
The management of PTSD in people with learning difficulties is the same as that for people without. The psychological therapy must of course 
be tailored to the ability of the patient.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding XYY syndrome?

options.text: It is associated with an increased risk of learning disability
Affected individuals are typically smaller than average
It corresponds to a karyotype of 45, XYY
It is also known as Kleinfelter's syndrome
It is associated with high levels of infertility

correct_answer.text: It is associated with an increased risk of learning disability

questions.explanation:
XYY syndrome 
XYY syndrome (sometimes referred to as 'super-males') is a condition where males possess an extra Y chromosome, producing 
the 47, XYY karyotype. 
 
It is usually asymptomatic. Affected individuals tend to be taller than average. Testosterone levels are normal and fertility and 
sexual development are usually unaffected.  
 
There is an increased risk of learning difficulties. Aggression is not seen in higher levels than the normal population.

questions.question_text: What percentage of Japanese children are estimated to have a reading ability delayed by one year?
questions.explanation:
Pretty random question, never the less it came up in the exam! 
Reading difficiulties in Japan 
The incidence of the reading disabilities among 250 Japanese children (8.5-13.4 years old) was measured by a standardized reading ability 
test which had recently been developed. It was found that 16.4% of the children tested have a one year delay, and 15.2% of the children have 
a two year delay. The results showed that Makita's (1968) claim concerning the rarity of the incidence of reading disabilities in Japan is 
incorrect.

Individuals with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome are usually of short stature and have some degree of intellectual disability.

People with LD have been found to have higher rates of generalised anxiety disorder when compared to the

correct_answer.text: People with LD have been found to have higher rates of generalised anxiety disorder when compared to the

questions.explanation:
compared to the general population 
Learning disability (anxiety disorders) 
Anxiety disorders are well recognised in people with learning disorders. The following research findings are significant:- 
 Higher rates of anxiety have been found in elderly individuals with LD compared to younger age groups 
 People with LD have higher rates of phobic disorder compared with the general population 
 People with LD have been found to have higher rates of generalised anxiety disorder when compared to the general population 
 
Diagnosis of anxiety disorders is complicated in patients with LD. As a general rule, criteria for anxiety disorders from the ICD-10 and DSM-IV 
can be applied to patients with mild to moderate LD. Patients with severe LD are best assed using behavioural equivalents. 
 
Management tends to parallel those used for the general population.

manage finances, attend to personal safety etc). Borderline learning disability is not generally associated with deficits in adaptive functioning.

The term 'borderline learning disability' is used to refer to people with an IQ in the range of 70-85 (recall that mild learning disability = IQ in

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome, key points 
 Inheritance is X-linked 
 Mutation of the FMR1 gene 
 Excessive trinucleotide repeats (CGG) 
 Women can be mildly affected 
 Length of trinucleotide repeat sequence correlates with the amount of cognitive impairment 
Fragile X Syndrome 
Fragile X is a genetic syndrome characterised by mental retardation, an elongated face, large protruding ears, and large testicles (in men). 
They tend to be shy, avoid eye contact, and have difficulties reading facial expressions. They often display stereotypic movements such as 
hand flapping. 
 
Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of learning disability. 
 
The speech of affected individuals of often abnormal. Of note are abnormalities of fluency (flow). Such speech is often referred to as cluttered. 
 
It is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by the amplification of a CGG repeat in the 5 untranslated region of the fragile X mental retardation 
1 gene (FMR1). These CGG repeats disrupt synthesis of the fragile X protein (FMRP) known to be essential for brain function and growth. The 
gene is located at Xq27. As with other trinucleotide repeat disorders (Huntington's, myotonic dystrophy, Friedreich's ataxia, and 
spinocerebellar ataxia) the greater number of repeats the more severe the condition. 
 
The fragile X phenotype typically involves a variety of psychiatric symptoms, including features of autism, attention deficit/hyperactivity 
disorder, anxiety, and aggression.  
 
Females as well as males are affected. This is through the process of X-inactivation, where one X in each female cell inactivates itself. Males 
are more severely affected because they have only one X chromosome. 
 
It has a prevalence estimate of 1/3600-4000.

questions.explanation:
William's syndrome is caused by a deletion from chromosome 7. Those affected tend to have cognitive impairment and are very social with 
surprisingly good language skills.Hyperacusis is common but individuals tend to have a love of music and can be very proficient in this area.It 
is associated with endocrine abnormalities, hypercalcemia particularly. 
William's syndrome 
William's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a distinctive elfin facial appearance, cheerful demeanour, low nasal 
bridge, and mild to moderate mental retardation. Individuals with the syndrome tend to be very sociable and highly verbal. 
 
The syndrome is caused by a deletion from the region q11.23 on chromosome 7. The deleted region codes for more than 20 genes. The 
deletion tends to take place during the recombination phase of meiosis. It can be detected by the use of fluorescent in situ hybridization 
(FISH).The syndrome is very rare with a prevalence of around 1 in 20000.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding Angelman syndrome?

options.text: It is caused by deleted material from the maternal chromosome
It results from deletions from chromosome 12

correct_answer.text: It is caused by deleted material from the maternal chromosome

questions.explanation:
Genomic imprinting 
Genomic imprinting refers to a situation where a piece of DNA can behave differently depending on whether it is inherited from the mother or 
the father. DNA sequences are marked (imprinted) in the ovaries and testes almost like a stamp which says where the sequence has come 
from, this stamp affects the expression of the sequence. The two classic examples in psychiatry include Prader-Willi and Angelman syndrome. 
 
Prader-Willi is due to a deletion of chromosome 15q when inherited from the father. It is characterised by hypotonia, short stature, 
polyphagia, obesity, small gonads, and mild mental retardation. 
 
Angelman's syndrome (Happy puppet syndrome) is due to a deletion of 15q when inherited from the mother. It is characterised by an 
unusually happy demeanour, developmental delay, seizures, sleep disturbance, and jerky hand movements.

William's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a distinctive elfin facial appearance, cheerful demeanour, low nasal

The syndrome is caused by a deletion from the region q11.23 on chromosome 7. The deleted region codes for more than 20 genes. The 
deletion tends to take place during the recombination phase of meiosis. It can be detected by the use of fluorescent in situ hybridization 
(FISH). 
 
The syndrome is very rare with a prevalence of around 1 in 20000.

questions.question_text: A couple have one child with Down's syndrome. What would increase the chance of their second child having Down's?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Jun 2010 
 
Most cases of Down syndrome are not inherited. When the condition is caused by trisomy 21, the chromosomal abnormality occurs as a 
random event during nondisjunction. Mosaic Down syndrome is also not inherited. It occurs as a random event during cell division early in fetal 
development.  
 
Translocation Down syndrome can be inherited. An unaffected person can carry a rearrangement of genetic material between chromosome 21 
and another chromosome. This rearrangement is called a balanced translocation because there is no extra material from chromosome 21. 
Although they do not have signs of Down syndrome, people who carry this type of balanced translocation are at an increased risk of having 
children with the condition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would lead you to suspect a diagnosis of Turner syndrome?
Which of the following is the closet approximation of the prevalence of schizophrenia in people with learning disabilities?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2015 
Schizophrenia (epidemiology) 
The epidemiological data on schizophrenia varies widely. Below are some important studies and their findings. You need to have an idea of 
the values. It is import to recognise however that compared to findings from other multifactoral conditions such as heart disease the magnitude 
of the differences across the studies is relatively small. 
 
Prevalence 
 
In a review of recent studies, Jablensky (2000) placed the prevalence rate in the range of 1.4-4.6 per thousand. 
 
Incidence 
 
Eaton (1999) presented data from 27 studies of schizophrenia published since 1985. The median incidence rate was 0.16 per thousand which 
was lower than previously reported. 
 
Gender 
 
The male female ratio is 1:1. 
 
Course and prognosis 
 
Schizophrenia is a chronic condition that tends to take a deteriorating course. The longer the follow up extends, the proportion classed as 
having a good outcome becomes the smaller.  
 
Many studies find that younger patients, males, and those with a positive family history have the worst outcome. 
 
Failure to comply with treatment has been shown to be one of the strongest predictors of relapse. 
 
Ram (1992) concluded that over a 2 year period, one-third of patients with schizophrenia showed a benign course, and two-thirds either 
relapsed or failed to recover. 
 
People with schizophrenia have a 2-3 fold increased risk of premature death (SMR all cause mortality 2.5). 
 
Winter births 
 
Winter births are associated with an increased risk of schizophrenia. 
 
Urbanicity 
 
There is a higher incidence associated with urbanicity. 
 
Migration 
 
There is a higher incidence associated with migration. 
 
Class 
 
Higher prevalence among lower socio-economic class. 
 
Learning disability 
 
Prevalence rates for schizophrenia in people with learning disabilities are approximately three times greater than for the general population 
(3% vs 1%) (Doody et al, 1998)

questions.question_text: A man undergoes intelligence testing to determine if a learning disability is present. He obtains a Full Scale IQ of 73. His psychiatrist questions the reliability of the result as they note that the test was normed many years ago and so the result may over estimate the man's actual ability. Which phenomenon underpins the psychiatrists argument?
questions.explanation:
Testing effect - the finding that long-term memory is increased when some of the learning period is devoted to retrieving the to-be-
remembered information through testing with proper feedback 
 
Ben Franklin effect - A person who has performed a favor for someone is more likely to do another favour for that person than they would be if 
they had received a favour from that person. 
 
DunningKruger effect - a cognitive bias in which relatively unskilled persons suffer illusory superiority, mistakenly assessing their ability to be 
much higher than it really is. 
 
Novelty effect - the tendency for an individual to have the strongest stress response the first time that individual is faced with a potentially 
threatening experience. Over time, as the novelty wears off, the stress response decreases. 
 
Flynn Effect 
The 'Flynn effect' refers to the observed rise over time in standardised intelligence test scores.  
 
Flynns study revealed a 13.8-point increase in IQ scores between 1932 and 1978, amounting to a 0.3-point increase per year, or 
approximately 3 points per decade. More recently, the Flynn effect was supported by calculations of IQ score gains between 1972 and 2006. 
 
The Flynn effect implies that an individual will likely attain a higher IQ score on an earlier version of a test than on the current version. In fact, a 
test will overestimate an individuals IQ score by an average of about 0.3 points per year between the year in which the test was normed and 
the year in which the test was administered.

Associated disorder Prevalence

 Major depressive disorder occurs and can be diagnosed at all IQ levels though the diagnosis is easily missed or simply seen as 
challenging behaviour. 
 People with learning disabilities are more vulnerable to the adverse effects of loss life events, and so more likely to develop 
adjustment disorder.

and autism where they may precipitate tics.

questions.question_text: In the case of an adult with a learning disability who develops an affective disorder, before starting lithium which of the following baseline investigations needs to be done?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Apr 2013 
Exam Question Aug 2008 
 
This question creates a lot of controversy, probably due to the fact that it is poorly written so don't worry too much about it.  
 
Some other sources suggest that EEG is the correct answer, this probably relates to a paragraph written in a set of 
guidelines called the 'Frith Prescribing Guidelines' written as a one of edition in 2005. 
 
In those guidelines it is suggested that an EEG is required before starting lithium as it can lower the seizure threshold and 
this is particularly relevant in those with LD as they are prone to seizures. This one off recommendation has not been 
supported by either NICE or the Maudsley Guidelines and so is best view with some caution.  
 
NICE and the Maudsley do however make it clear that all people should have an ECG before starting lithium, so if you pick 
that answer you can't go wrong. 
Lithium (before prescribing) 
Before prescribing lithium the following must be checked:- 
 Renal function 
 Cardiac function 
 Thyroid function 
 
In addition, women of childbearing age should be advised regarding contraception, and information about toxicity should be provided. 
 
Patients should be warned that bouts of vomiting/ diarrhoea (or any dehydration) will increase lithium levels.A salt free diet is contraindicated. 
Lithium can also worsen psoriasis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following results in a mutation of the HPRT1 gene?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Oct 2013 
Lesch-Nyan Syndrome 
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a condition characterised by the overproduction and accumulation of uric acid. People with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome 
usually cannot walk, require assistance sitting, and are generally wheelchair-bound. Self-injury, including biting and head banging, is the most 
common and distinctive behavioral problem in those with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. 
 
Mutations in the HPRT1 gene cause Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Mutations in the HPRT1 gene cause a severe deficiency of the enzyme 
hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase 1. This enzyme is responsible for recycling purines, a type of building block of DNA and its chemical 
cousin RNA. When this enzyme is lacking, the breakdown of purines results in abnormally high levels of uric acid in the body. The condition is 
inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.

Which of the following is recommended as first line treatment in the management of obsessive compulsive disorder in a child with a mild learning difficulty?
questions.explanation:
The recommendations for OCD are broadly similar for adults and young people (with or without learning difficulties). Psychological therapy (be 
it self help or CBT with ERP) is always first line, failing that an SSRI should be used. 
 
Having a learning difficulty should not limit a persons access to psychological therapy. Of course a severe learning disability may mean it is 
not possible but tailored forms of CBT can be effective for less severe forms. 
OCD in young people (NICE Guidelines) 
NICE suggest the following on the management of OCD in young people 
 Mild - Guided self help, if no improvement try CBT with ERP 
 Moderate / severe - CBT with ERP (first), then consider combined treatments of CBT (including ERP) with SSRI, alternative SSRI or 
clomipramine 
 
ERP refers to exposure and response prevention. This is a psychological method which involves exposing a patient to an anxiety provoking 
situation (e.g. for someone with OCD, having dirty hands) and then stopping them engaging in their usual safety behavior (e.g. washing their 
hands). This helps them confront their anxiety and the habituation leads to eventual extinction of the response. 
 
NICE recommend using sertraline and fluvoxamine for OCD in young people. 
 
If the child also has depression then fluoxetine is suggested. 
 
Clomipramine is suggested as second line.  
 
Treatment should be continued for at least 6 months from the beginning of remission.

Lyonization always occurs in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Exam Question Apr 2014 
 
Klinefelters syndrome is caused by the presence of one or more extra copies of the X chromosome in a male's cells. Extra genetic 
material from the X chromosome interferes with male sexual development, preventing the testes from functioning normally and 
reducing the levels of testosterone. A shortage of testosterone can lead to delayed or incomplete puberty, genital abnormalities, 
gynecomastia, reduced facial and body hair, and infertility. Affected individuals may also have learning disabilities, delayed speech 
and language development, and a shy and unassuming personality. 
 
Typically, people with Klinefelters syndrome have one extra copy of the X chromosome in each cell, (a total of two X chromosomes 
and one Y chromosome referred to as 47,XXY). Less commonly, affected individuals may have two or three extra X chromosomes 
(48,XXXY or 49,XXXXY). As the number of extra sex chromosomes increases, so does the risk of learning problems, intellectual 
disability, birth defects, and other issues. 
 
Some people with features of Klinefelters syndrome have the extra X chromosome in only some of their cells (mosaic). Individuals 
with mosaic Klinefelters syndrome may have milder signs and symptoms, depending on how many cells have an additional X 
chromosome. 
 
Lyonization occurs when there are more than one X chromosomes in a cell. For this reason Lyonization occurs to some degree in all 
people affected with Klinefelters syndrome. 
Lyonization 
The X chromosome contains over 1,000 genes that are essential for proper development and cell viability. Females carry two copies of the X 
chromosome, resulting in a potentially toxic double dose of X-linked genes. To correct this imbalance, by way of the process called 
Lyonization (X-inactivation), females transcriptionally silence one of their two Xs. The inactivated X chromosome then condenses into a 
compact structure called a Barr body, which is maintained in a silent state. 
 
The process of X-inactivation is random. There is no preference for the inactivation of paternal or maternal X chromosomes. It occurs very 
early in embryogenesis, soon after the fertilization of the egg by the sperm (when the dividing conceptus about 16-32 cells big). 
 
It occurs in every female cell. X inactivation affects most but not all genes on the X chromosome. If cell has more than two X chromosomes 
then the extra Xs are also inactivated.
